title: Ezekiel 3:22–27
context: The LORD’s hand comes on the prophet again, and he is told to go out into the plain (3:22). There he sees the LORD’s glory, “like the glory which I saw by the river Chebar”, and falls on his face (3:23). The Spirit sets him on his feet, and the LORD tells him, “Go, shut yourself inside your house” (3:24). The LORD says “they will put ropes on you, and will bind you with them” (3:25), and the LORD will make his tongue stick to the roof of his mouth so that he will be mute and “will not be able to correct them” (3:26). Yet when the LORD speaks with him, he will open his mouth, and the prophet will say, “This is what the Lord GOD says” (3:27). The muteness is presented as a sign from the LORD, and later the book reports the prophet’s mouth opened when a survivor brings news that the city has been defeated (compare 24:25–27 and 33:21–22). Readers differ on who binds him (the exiles, or a figurative binding) and on how the muteness fits with the oracles he speaks in between; a common reading takes it as a restriction to speaking only when the LORD gives a word. The text presents the binding and muteness as the LORD’s doing. Both traditions read the unit as shared ground: the prophet’s speech and silence are both under the LORD’s command.

verses.text: The LORD’s hand was there on me; and he said to me, “Arise, go out into the plain, and I will talk with you there.”
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD’s hand was there on me”, and the prophet is told to go out into the plain. Arminian readers note that the LORD draws the prophet aside before giving the next instruction. The pattern of hand, command, and obedience continues from chapter 1.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s initiative in calling the prophet apart to speak with him. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a new scene within the commissioning, and neither presses the location of the plain beyond what the text says.

verses.text: Then I arose, and went out into the plain, and behold, the LORD’s glory stood there, like the glory which I saw by the river Chebar. Then I fell on my face.
verses.arminianNotes: In the plain the prophet sees the LORD’s glory, “like the glory which I saw by the river Chebar”, and falls on his face. Arminian readers note that the same glory meets him again. The commission is renewed in the same awe that began it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see continuity: the God who called the prophet by the Chebar is present in the plain. Shared ground: both traditions read the prophet’s falling down as fitting reverence, and both see the glory as the authority behind the hard instructions that follow.

verses.text: Then the Spirit entered into me and set me on my feet. He spoke with me, and said to me, “Go, shut yourself inside your house.
verses.arminianNotes: “Then the Spirit entered into me and set me on my feet”, as in 2:2, and the LORD says, “Go, shut yourself inside your house.” Arminian readers note that the Spirit’s enabling comes before a hard command, and the prophet is equipped to obey it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the Spirit preparing the prophet for a sign of restriction. Shared ground: both traditions read the Spirit’s work here as the same enabling seen in 2:2, not as a point of dispute, and both see the confinement as part of the prophet’s sign-ministry.

verses.text: But you, son of man, behold, they will put ropes on you, and will bind you with them, and you will not go out among them.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “they will put ropes on you, and will bind you with them, and you will not go out among them.” Arminian readers note that the text does not say who binds him. Some take it as hostility from the exiles, others as a figurative binding; the verse leaves it open.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the uncertainty over who binds the prophet and whether the ropes are literal or figurative. Shared ground: both traditions read the binding as part of a sign that the LORD directs, and both decline to settle what the text does not specify.

verses.text: I will make your tongue stick to the roof of your mouth so that you will be mute and will not be able to correct them, for they are a rebellious house.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will make the prophet mute so that he “will not be able to correct them, for they are a rebellious house.” Arminian readers note that the silence itself is a judgment on the people. Readers differ on whether it limits all speech or only a role of correcting the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the muteness as a sign of judgment directed by the LORD, and many take it as limiting the prophet’s role as the people’s reprover. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse in its literary context, noting the later opening of his mouth (compare 33:22), and neither rests on medical theories.

verses.text: But when I speak with you, I will open your mouth, and you shall tell them, ‘This is what the Lord GOD says.’ He who hears, let him hear; and he who refuses, let him refuse; for they are a rebellious house.”
verses.arminianNotes: “But when I speak with you, I will open your mouth”. Arminian readers note that the prophet’s silence is broken only by the LORD’s word. The LORD opens it so that the prophet can say, “This is what the Lord GOD says.” The people may then hear or refuse, and the choice set before them is real.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see that the prophet speaks only as the LORD opens his mouth, so the word is wholly God’s. Shared ground: both traditions read the closing formula as placing responsibility on the hearers, and both see it echoing the hear-or-refuse refrain of 2:5, 2:7, and 3:11.
